title: The refractory period
summary: After a spike, the neuron cannot fire again until it recovers.

terms.plain: the forced quiet after a spike
terms.definition: A short time after a spike during which the neuron cannot fire again, or can fire only with a much stronger input.
The highest spike rate a neuron can reach, set by how long it must wait between spikes.
The input is so strong that the neuron is already firing as fast as the refractory period allows. Extra input does not raise the rate.

cards.text:
Right after a spike, the neuron is briefly unavailable.
That forced quiet is the refractory period.

cards.lead: A neuron must wait 5 ms between spikes.
lines: In one second there are 1000 ms.
The fastest it can tip is 1000 ÷ 5 = 200 times.
That ceiling is its maximum firing rate.

cards.text:
Past that ceiling, a harder input changes nothing.
The rate has saturated.

question.prompt: The neuron must wait 5 ms between spikes. What is the maximum number of spikes in one second?
question.simpler: Divide one second by the wait between spikes.

question.prompt: Once the rate has saturated, a stronger input still produces more spikes.
question.why: The refractory period is already the limit. Extra input cannot slip a spike into the quiet gap.
question.simpler: Saturation means the rate has stopped rising.

recall.question: What sets a neuron’s maximum firing rate?
recall.answer: The refractory period, the forced wait between spikes.

deeper.note: Sodium channels need time to recover after a spike. That is the biological refractory period. A leaky integrate-and-fire model adds the same pause by hand. Hodgkin and Huxley measured the currents. Gerstner’s Neuronal Dynamics, section 1.3, shows the pause in the simple model.

paper.title: A quantitative description of membrane current and its application to conduction and excitation in nerve
paper.section: Sodium inactivation is why a real axon cannot fire again immediately.
